title: The Patient Hymn
premise: Beatrix Galloway, a rationalist property surveyor, is sent to appraise Hollowmere House, a decaying manor whose rooms measure differently each time she walks them. The house is a counting machine: it tallies its residents, and when the count reaches a number it remembers from 1911, it will 'ring' — pulling everyone inside into the drowned hour when the original bell, the villagers, and the family who owned it all vanished. Beatrix moves in with the Vane family, the reluctant heirs, and slowly realizes her own missing childhood summer is stitched into the house's memory. As the bell tolls closer to its final count, Beatrix must choose between the found family she's built with the Vanes and the erased family the house keeps trying to give back to her; in the end she breaks the count by giving the house a memory it never had — a name for the unnamed child — and the bell falls silent, though Beatrix leaves Hollowmere knowing some part of her will always still be inside, counting.
about_author: Elodie Hartwell is the pen name of a former archivist who spent a decade cataloguing deeds and estate records in the English countryside, where she became convinced that houses remember more than the people who live in them. She writes horror about bureaucracy, inheritance, and the terrible patience of old buildings.

chapters.title: The Measurement Problem
chapters.summary: Beatrix Galloway arrives at Hollowmere House to appraise it for sale, armed with laser measures and professional detachment. The hallway measures 4.2 meters on her first pass and 4.6 on her second. She blames the equipment. The beat is dry, controlled skepticism — a woman who trusts numbers more than people, meeting a house that lies in numbers.

chapters.title: The Vanes of Hollowmere
chapters.summary: Beatrix meets the Vane family: widowed matriarch Ivy, her prickly adult son Casper, and his quiet daughter Wren, who draws the same staircase over and over. They live in three rooms of a house built for twenty. Beatrix notes their codependence with clinical disapproval, but feels an unwanted pang watching Wren. The beat is wary observation softening into reluctant fascination.

chapters.title: A Bell That Was Melted Down
chapters.summary: In the village archive, Beatrix confirms the church bell was removed and melted in 1911 — yet that evening, across the moor, she hears it ring once. The Vanes go pale and begin checking the house room by room, counting aloud. Beatrix realizes they've heard it before. The beat is the first crack in her rationalism, masked as irritation.

chapters.title: The Count
chapters.summary: Casper explains the family curse: the house counts its people, and when the count matches 1911's — eleven souls, they believe — the bell will ring them into the hour the village lost. Ivy forbids discussion; Wren has already heard it ring twice. Beatrix, professionally offended, decides the family is mentally unwell. The beat is dread arriving secondhand, disbelieved.

chapters.title: Rooms That Remember
chapters.summary: Beatrix surveys the east wing and finds a nursery that appears on no floor plan, wallpaper patterned with tally marks. Her instruments fail; her own handwriting in her survey notes reads 'she is still here.' She sleeps badly, dreaming of a summer she can't place. The beat is uncanny erosion — the professional's tools turning against her.

chapters.title: Wren's Drawings
chapters.summary: Wren shows Beatrix forty drawings of the staircase, each adding a figure on the steps — and the newest drawing includes a woman with a clipboard. Wren says, 'You were already here when I was little.' Beatrix's missing summer at an aunt's house surfaces as a blank, screaming gap. The beat is vertigo: memory as a locked room.

chapters.title: The Parish Register
chapters.summary: Beatrix digs into 1911: the Ashcombe family, eleven members, vanished the night the bell rang its last; the village woke with a church that had no bell and a manor with no family. One name in the register is smudged — a child recorded only as 'the foundling.' Beatrix feels the smudge like a wound. The beat is obsession taking root.

chapters.title: Three Rings at Dawn
chapters.summary: The bell rings three times before dawn. The Vanes count themselves: four. Beatrix realizes her presence has changed the count's arithmetic, and Ivy, terrified, asks her to leave. Casper defends her. Wren holds Beatrix's hand and says the house 'likes' her. The beat is found family forming inside a threat — belonging as danger.

chapters.title: What Ivy Buried
chapters.summary: Ivy confesses: her husband didn't die abroad; he walked into the house's west stairwell in 1999 and never came out, and she has kept the family in three rooms ever since, refusing the house its count. Beatrix recognizes the arithmetic of grief. The beat is two kinds of denial meeting — Ivy's and Beatrix's own.

chapters.title: The West Stairwell
chapters.summary: Against Ivy's pleas, Beatrix and Casper open the sealed stairwell. Inside, the air is 1911: gaslight, hymnals, a table set for eleven. Casper finds his father's coat, still warm. The bell tolls once more — five. The beat is awe curdling into horror; the house is not haunting them, it is preserving them.

chapters.title: Hollowmere's Hour
chapters.summary: Beatrix theorizes: the house is a reliquary replaying the hour of the vanishing, and each ring pulls the present closer to the past. Wren begins sleepwalking to the nursery, speaking in a voice not her own, counting in a child's cadence. The beat is the family fracturing under the strain — love stretched across a century.

chapters.title: The Foundling
chapters.summary: Beatrix's blocked summer returns in fragments: she was the foundling's grandniece, fostered at Hollowmere one childhood summer, and the house has been waiting for her to come back and finish the count. She remembers a name the register smudged because no one ever gave the child one. The beat is devastating recognition — she is not surveying the house; she is its missing piece.

chapters.title: Six, Seven
chapters.summary: Two rings in one night. The village evacuates; a skeptical vicar's assistant, Nell Okafor, arrives to investigate and becomes an ally, bringing outside records: the foundling died in 1911, before the vanishing, and was never named — which is why the count never closed. The beat is grim clarity: the house is stuck mid-grief, ringing for a child no one mourned by name.

chapters.title: Ivy's Refusal
chapters.summary: Ivy, learning the count can only close with a death or a name, chooses the house's terms: she will give herself to the stairwell to stop the rings from taking Wren. Casper and Beatrix physically bar her way. The beat is the family's darkest night — sacrifice mistaken for the only door.

chapters.title: The Nursery Tally
chapters.summary: Beatrix enters the nursery alone and reads the wallpaper tallies: hundreds of counts across a century, each ring a rehearsal. In the corner, a child's handwriting has written the same unfinished sentence for a hundred years: 'My name is —'. The beat is heartbreak at the center of the horror: an eternity of waiting to be called something.

chapters.title: Nine
chapters.summary: The bell rings nine times; the house begins folding 1911 into the present — gaslight in the halls, hymn-singing behind walls, the Ashcombe family's shadows setting the table. Wren is speaking only in the child's voice now. Nell warns they have days at most. The beat is the walls between times thinning; dread becoming countdown.

chapters.title: The Argument at the Table
chapters.summary: The Vanes and Beatrix fight over the endgame: run and let the house take its eleven from whoever remains, or stay and solve it. Casper accuses Beatrix of wanting the house to want her; she realizes he's right — the found family she's built is the first she's ever had, and she'd rather haunt with them than be whole without them. The beat is love confessed as selfishness.

chapters.title: Ten
chapters.summary: Ten rings. The village church's empty bell tower begins to hum. Wren, fully claimed by the child's voice, walks to the west stairwell, and Ivy follows her in. Beatrix and Casper pursue them into 1911's preserved hour, where the Ashcombes' shadows turn to look at them with patient faces. The beat is the point of no return — inside the house's memory.

chapters.title: The Drowned Hour
chapters.summary: Inside the repeated hour, Beatrix finds Ivy holding Wren at the table set for eleven. The child's shadow waits at the empty place, unfinished sentence hovering. Beatrix understands: the count isn't a trap, it's a christening that never happened — the house cannot close a number that never got its name. The beat is terrible compassion.

chapters.title: A Name for the Unnamed
chapters.summary: At the climax, as the bell begins its final peal, Beatrix gives the foundling a name — her own middle name, given freely, written in the register and spoken aloud in the nursery: 'Your name is Beatrice.' The tally wallpaper completes its last mark; the shadows bow; Ivy and Wren return to the present. The eleventh ring never falls. The beat is grief answered with gift.

chapters.title: Silence, Then Birds
chapters.summary: The house exhales: rooms settle to their true measurements, the west stairwell becomes an ordinary stair, the nursery wallpaper is blank. Ivy weeps over her husband's coat, finally cold, finally buried. The bell tower is silent. Beatrix, changed, no longer disbelieves — but believes differently now. The beat is release and quiet mourning.

chapters.title: The Appraisal
chapters.summary: Weeks later, Beatrix files her survey: Hollowmere House, structurally sound, recommended for retention by the family. The Vanes ask her to stay — not as surveyor, but as family — and she does, taking the room that used to be the nursery. On her last walk through, she counts the residents aloud: five. The house, for the first time, agrees. The beat is found family sealed, memory carried forward instead of drowned.
